title: Response-size Bucketing and Adaptive Rate Protocol for Throughput Runs
body:
Summary:

This note documents a complementary methodology for throughput benchmarking focused on response-size stratification and adaptive request-rate bucketing. The approach is intended to improve run repeatability across variable-length generation workloads and to make throughput comparisons between model variants and quantization paths more robust to noise introduced by tail latencies, thermal effects, and platform scheduling.

Motivation and problem statement:

Many production workloads have a broad distribution of generation lengths (short replies, medium completions, long-form). A single aggregate QPS target or a single arrival pattern can hide path-dependent performance characteristics: e.g., long-tail token generation can amplify GPU memory pressure, increase KV cache churn, and push different kernel dispatch paths. Existing staircase/warmup playbooks are useful, but runs still vary when the response length mix changes between experiments.

Goals:

- Produce repeatable throughput estimates that are stable across reruns and small platform drift.
- Surface sensitivity to response-size mix (short/medium/long) as a first-class dimension.
- Provide a light-weight adaptive bucketing layer so load generators can maintain target occupancy without saturating the system abruptly.
- Reduce run-to-run noise with anchor requests and percentile anchoring rather than mean-only signals.

High-level approach:

1) Profile the workload offline to produce a response-length fingerprint: a small sample of representative prompts that produce short (<32 tokens), medium (32–256 tokens), and long (>256 tokens) completions.

2) Create buckets for each response-size class. Each bucket has its own rate schedule and warmup curve. Buckets are mixed at the client according to a `mix` vector matching the target workload, but each bucket is driven independently so we can measure per-bucket throughput and latency.

3) Within each bucket use an adaptive rate controller that targets a desired occupancy metric (e.g., GPU active tokens/s or model concurrency) instead of raw QPS. This controller slowly increases offered rate until a knee is detected. Knee detection uses percentile latency growth (p90 and p99 slope) and GPU scheduling backpressure signals.

4) Anchor the run with periodic deterministic probe requests (a small set of synthetic prompts that are highly repeatable). These anchors run at low frequency throughout the experiment to detect drift and permit cross-run alignment.

Load generator design details:

- Bucketing: 3 buckets = short, medium, long. Each bucket has:
  - id: "short|med|long"
  - sample_prompts: 20 seeded prompts that map to the length class (store in fixtures/response-buckets/)
  - stride: how many parallel clients to assign initially
  - per-bucket pacing: initial qps and max qps cap

- Adaptive rate controller (per-bucket):
  - Warmup stage: exponential growth from 1 RPS to 20% of target over 90s to allow kernel caching and allocator stabilization.
  - Ramp stage: linear increase from 20% -> 100% over configurable window (default 10 minutes).
  - Control rule: if p90 latency increases by >15% between two sampling windows OR GPU queue depth / pending requests grows by >20% then decrease rate by 12% and hold for one stability window. If p90 stable and GPU util < target, increase by 6%.
  - Safety caps: if any GPU memory usage crosses 92% or CUDA OOM occurs, abort the run and flag for investigation.

- Percentile anchoring and trimming: compute p50/p90/p99 per-bucket and global. For reporting use trimmed-mean throughput (drop top and bottom 5% of sliding windows) and report both median and trimmed-mean. Avoid using simple mean token/sec as the only signal.

Anchors and checkpoints:

- Deterministic anchors: inject one anchor request every 30s per host (low volume). Anchors are static seeded prompts that traverse the same codepath and should be deterministic across model versions where semantics unchanged. Use anchor latency to align timelines between runs and detect thermal drift.

- Checkpoints: capture a checkpoint every 3 minutes: snapshot of GPU metrics (util, mem, temp), host CPU load, number of outstanding requests, and per-bucket p90. Store these to object storage with run id for post-run analysis.

Thermal and driver noise mitigation:

- Avoid back-to-back benchmark runs on the same hardware when possible. If unavoidable, insert a 15–30 minute cooldown or a synthetic idling period with small anchor traffic to let temperatures normalize.

- Record thermal sensors and driver version; include process-level cgroups/affinity so we can correlate OS scheduling noise.

Reproducibility checklist (pre-run):

- [ ] Confirm model binary and quantization flags.
- [ ] Confirm kernel selection pins (if any) and runtime environment variables.
- [ ] Reserve GPUs exclusively for the run or use dedicated capacity mode.
- [ ] Upload bucket fixtures (seeded prompts) to the harness artifact store and reference them by checksum.
- [ ] Schedule run start aligned to NTP-synced clock and note run-id.
- [ ] Warm-up the model with micro-primer (see warmup recipe below).

Warmup recipe (micro-primer + steady primer):

1) Micro-primer (3–5 minutes): single-threaded sequence of anchor prompts across all buckets to populate caches and kernel JIT caches. No concurrency, low QPS.
2) Concurrency primer (10 minutes): bring up per-bucket clients to 10% of target concurrency; ensure steady allocation of KV cache and confirm memory plateau.
3) Staircase ramp (5–10 minutes): increase to 50% and then to 80% with short holds at each step (60s). After this stage start adaptive rate controller.

Run duration and analysis windows:

- Minimum steady-state window: 20 minutes after reaching stable-adaptive state. This ensures capture of thermal and scheduling cycles.
- For final throughput numbers, compute metrics over the last 15 minutes of the steady-state window. Use the anchored trimmed-mean throughput and report per-bucket p50/p90/p99.

Failure modes and diagnostics:

- OOMs: capture model allocator logs, increase logging verbosity for that run, rerun with reduced concurrency and compare per-bucket memory footprints.
- Run-to-run drift: compare anchor latencies; if median anchor latency differs by >7% across runs, mark runs as non-comparable and investigate thermal or driver changes.
- High variance but stable median: inspect contention on host network, GC pauses, context switches; correlate host-level vmstat / iostat and perf counters.

Example run manifest (human readable):

run_id: resp-bucket-20241107-01
model: gptx-13b-quant-v2
buckets:
  - id: short, mix: 0.5, target_tokens_per_sec: 10k
  - id: med, mix: 0.35, target_tokens_per_sec: 18k
  - id: long, mix: 0.15, target_tokens_per_sec: 36k
anchor_probe_interval: 30s
checkpoint_interval: 180s
warmup: micro-primer(5m)->concurrency-primer(10m)->staircase(5m)
adaptive_controller: enabled
metrics_to_capture: [gpu_util, gpu_mem, p50/p90/p99, tokens/sec_by_bucket, anchors, host_cpu]

Post-run artifacts and analysis checklist:

- Raw loadgen traces (per-request latencies and sizes) saved to object storage.
- GPU telemetry and checkpoints.
- Anchor time series and checksum of anchor fixture used.
- Run summary CSV with per-bucket trimmed-mean throughput and percentiles.
- Comparison diff against baseline run-id and flagging of significant regressions (>5% throughput or >10% p90).

Open questions and TODOs:

- Determine best canonical bucket cutpoints for our most common customer workloads (produce a catalog).
- Explore automated mix resynthesis: given a customer RPS trace, synthesize an optimal bucket mix rather than sampling.
- Evaluate whether anchors can be made semantic-stable across model-family changes (fall-back anchors for incompatible models).

Notes and references:

- See related experiments: bench-harness/response-fingerprint-experiments (internal repo).
- This method is intentionally conservative: we prioritize signal clarity over micro-optimistic max throughput claims. Use it for engineering comparisons and SLA forecasting, not marketing headline numbers.

Contact: Eleanor Chen (eng-serving-runtime) for run templates, fixtures, and harness scripts.
